blocks.text: ==Caching== stores a copy of a response so a later request can **reuse** it instead of hitting the origin.

items: Lower **latency**: no round trip to origin
Less **bandwidth**: fewer bytes cross the wire
Less **origin load**: servers do less work
==Shared cache== (CDN, proxy): serves many users
==Private cache== (browser): serves one user
Each layer stops the trip if it holds a copy

blocks.note: Age: time since the origin sent or revalidated it

items: Here: 600 − 120 = **480s** of freshness left
At Age 600 the copy turns stale
Stale ≠ unusable: **revalidate** it, or serve under explicit stale rules
No lifetime set? ==Heuristic freshness== guesses ~**10%** of (Date − Last-Modified)
Last-Modified 30 days ago → fresh about 3 days

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Hit = fast. Miss = origin. Fresh = reuse. Stale = revalidate. Next: Cache-Control sets the lifetime.

items: `Cache-Control` is the modern header that governs caching
It ==overrides== `Expires` and `Pragma` when present
Syntax: comma-separated directives
`Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600`
`max-age=N`: fresh for ==N seconds== after generation
Clock starts at the `Date` header, not receipt
Cache subtracts `Age` header from the lifetime
`max-age=0` means stale at once: **revalidate** each use
`s-maxage=N` applies only to ==shared caches==
It also lets shared caches store responses with `Authorization`
Private browser cache ignores it
Counting max-age from receipt, ignoring `Age`
Relying on `Pragma: no-cache` in responses
Setting `Expires` and expecting it to win
Response is 40s old at the CDN: `Age: 40`
With `max-age=60`, **20s** of freshness remain
With `s-maxage=3600`, the CDN keeps it **3560s**

blocks.title: Debug tip
blocks.text: Run `curl -I` and compare `Age` with `max-age` to see what a cache will do.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: CDN uses s-maxage first, then max-age. Browsers only see max-age.

items: ==no-cache== does NOT mean don't cache
Response may be stored, but must be revalidated before every reuse
==no-store== means never write it to any cache
Not browser, not CDN, not proxy: nothing is kept
no-cache = caching plus a **freshness** guarantee
no-store = no caching at all
no-store: banking pages, tokens, personal data
no-cache: HTML shells, checked but a cheap 304
`must-revalidate`: once stale, no serving without a successful check
Applies even if the origin is down: cache returns 504
`no-cache, no-store` together is redundant
`no-store` alone is enough
Using **no-cache** as no-store for private data
That leaves a copy on disk in the cache
Trusting no-store to hide data from history or back-button
Skipping a real test of the page after logout
Revalidating HTML costs a cheap **304**, not a download
Sensitive pages skip the cache entirely

blocks.title: Test it
blocks.text: Log out, press Back, and check the page is gone. Use `curl -I` to read headers.

blocks.title: bfcache
blocks.text: Back/forward cache can restore a page whatever the headers say, unless no-store is set. Test it.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Secret? ==no-store==. Must be fresh but cacheable? ==no-cache==.

items: ==public==: any cache, even shared ones, may store it
`public` works even with Authorization or personalized look
==private==: only the user's browser may store it
CDNs and proxies **must not** keep a private copy

blocks.title: Authorization default
blocks.text: Responses to Authorization requests are NOT shared-cacheable unless `public`, `s-maxage` or `must-revalidate` is set.

items: ==immutable==: body never changes while fresh
Browser skips revalidation, even on reload
Normal reload sends a conditional request per asset
Safari/Firefox honor it; others **ignore** it safely
`stale-while-revalidate=N`: serve stale instantly, refresh in background
Hides revalidation latency from users
`stale-if-error=N`: serve stale if origin gives 5xx or is down

blocks.note: N = how stale you can tolerate

blocks.title: SWR trade-off
blocks.text: Users may see content up to max-age + N seconds old. Pick N by how stale is acceptable.

items: A ==validator== lets a cache ask "has this changed?" cheaply
Without it, a stale copy can only be **re-fetched** in full
`Last-Modified`: timestamp, 1-second resolution, HTTP date
`ETag`: opaque id of one representation version

blocks.note: ETag value is opaque, never parse it

items: Strong `"abc"`: byte-for-byte identical
Weak `W/"abc"`: semantically equivalent only
Generate from a content hash (MD5/SHA)
Or a version number, or inode+size+mtime
If both sent, caches use both
ETag **wins** for If-None-Match matching
Inode-based ETags differ per load-balanced node: needless 200s
Compression middleware may alter or strip the ETag
gzip vs br variants need ==distinct== ETags
`If-Range` and Range need **strong** validators; weak fails
Future or constantly changing Last-Modified breaks heuristic freshness
Hash the **content**, not the file's inode
Same bytes must give the same ETag on every node
Give each gzip/br variant its own ETag
Pair the validator with a `Cache-Control` lifetime

blocks.title: Check it
blocks.text: Run `curl -I` twice against two nodes: the ETag should match.

blocks.title: Pin it
blocks.text: No validator = full re-download every time.

items: Static files: send both, ETag wins on match
Dynamic pages: hash the rendered body
Range downloads: strong ETag only
Pair every validator with a `Cache-Control` lifetime
Weak ETag fails **If-Range**: full body is sent
Middleware that recompresses may weaken or strip the ETag
Constant Last-Modified updates on dynamic pages break ==heuristic freshness==
A future Last-Modified date confuses caches

blocks.title: Verify it
blocks.text: Send `curl -H 'If-None-Match: "v7"' -I` and expect a 304, not a 200.

items: Read the `ETag` from the first 200 response
Send it back as `If-None-Match`
Expect **304** with an empty body
Change the file, repeat, expect a new ETag and 200

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Hash the ==content==, send it on every node, and always pair it with a lifetime.

items: Send a validator on every cacheable response
Use strong ETags if Range requests matter
Keep Last-Modified as a cheap fallback for files
Test 304s with a normal reload, not a hard one

blocks.text: A ==conditional request== sends the stored __validator__ back to the origin. The origin answers **304** (no body) or **200** (fresh body).

blocks.title: Precedence
blocks.text: Both sent? If-None-Match wins; the date is ignored.

items: 304 should repeat `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `ETag`, `Vary`
Cache uses them to update stored freshness
Then it ==resets the freshness clock==
Serves its **stored** body to the user
One round trip, tiny headers only
Saves **bandwidth**, not latency
Still slower than a fresh hit (zero network)
If-Match / If-Unmodified-Since: optimistic concurrency on writes
Mismatch returns **412 Precondition Failed**
If-Range: resume only if the validator still matches
Otherwise server sends the full body, not a range
Server ignores `If-None-Match`, always **200**: wasted bandwidth
304 without a Vary-aware check: serves the wrong variant
Hard reload (Ctrl+Shift+R) skips cache, so it can't test 304s
Repeat `Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `ETag`, `Vary`
Cache merges them into the ==stored copy==
Then it **resets** the freshness clock
Missing headers leave the old lifetime in force

blocks.note: stored body is served, not this one

items: Test 304s with F5, never a hard reload
Check DevTools: status 304, tiny transfer size
Same variant must match: check `Vary` too
Server must honor `If-None-Match` before the date

blocks.title: Spot a broken 304
blocks.text: Reload twice. Still 200 with full size? The server ignores the validator.

lines: # tag belongs to the gzip copy
blocks.note: tag must match the same variant

items: A 304 is valid only for the **same variant**
Per-encoding ETags keep gzip and br apart
Cache stores the `Vary` list with the copy
Wrong match means a full **200**, not a 304
Read `If-None-Match`; if present, compare tags
Any listed tag matches: reply **304**
Only if absent, check `If-Modified-Since`
Otherwise send **200** with the fresh body

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Honor ==If-None-Match== first, match the same variant, and repeat the headers on every 304.

items: ==Vary== lists request headers that shaped the response
Cache key = URL **plus** those header values
Same URL, different header value = separate stored copy
Missing Vary is a correctness bug, not a tuning issue

blocks.note: Vary names the header to match

items: `Vary: Accept-Language` for localized pages
`Vary: Accept` for WebP vs JPEG negotiation
`Vary: *` means shared caches must always revalidate
A **304** must match the same variant (Vary applies there too)
No Vary: a gzip body reaches a client that cannot decode it
`Vary: Cookie` makes every session its own entry
`Vary: User-Agent`: normalize at the CDN instead
Personalised page on public URL without Vary or `private` leaks to other users
Normalize `Accept-Encoding` to gzip/br at the CDN
Whitelist only needed headers in the cache key
Put locale in the path: `/en/`, `/fr/`
Mark personalised pages `private` or `no-store`

blocks.title: Check it
blocks.text: Run `curl -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: br'` and read the `Vary` line.

blocks.title: Limit the variants
blocks.text: Whitelist or normalize headers in the CDN cache key. Better: use separate URLs (/en/, /fr/) over Vary.

slides.page_title: Browser vs CDN vs Proxy Caches

items: {icon:laptop} ==Browser==: private, per user and device, fastest, zero network
{icon:cloudfront} ==CDN edge==: shared by a region, offloads the origin
==Forward proxy==: in front of clients (corporate/ISP), shared by that group
==Reverse proxy== (Varnish, nginx, Cloudflare): in front of origins, serves all clients

spec.title: Request path, each layer with its own TTL

items: First layer with a fresh copy answers
Browser honors `private` and `no-store`
CDN honors `s-maxage` and `public`
You **cannot** purge browsers; CDNs yes
`CDN-Cache-Control`: standard CDN-only header
`Surrogate-Control`: Varnish/Fastly style
`Cloudflare-CDN-Cache-Control`: Cloudflare only
Each gives the CDN a policy browsers never see

lines: # on deploy: purge by tag or URL
blocks.note: browser revalidates, CDN holds a day

items: CDNs may ignore origin headers for some extensions
Some CDNs add their own **minimum** TTL
`301` is cached long, `302` follows its headers
A cached 301 traps users on the old target

blocks.title: Check first
blocks.text: Run `curl -I` and read Age plus X-Cache before blaming the origin.

slides.subtitle: Who caches where

caption.text: Your site is slow and you're blaming the server, but the real culprit is probably a cache header you got wrong. These handwritten notes break down HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag and 304s, the Vary header, browser vs CDN caches, hashed-filename busting, and the production misconfigurations that bite. Save this for your next deploy and send it to the dev who keeps shipping no-cache everywhere.
